			<span class=3D"posted-on">Posted on <a href=3D"https://lovelettertocolum=
bus.com/victorians-midnight-cafe/" rel=3D"bookmark"><time class=3D"entry-da=
te published" datetime=3D"2025-05-15T10:05:21-04:00"></time><time class=3D"=
updated" datetime=3D"2025-05-22T00:10:28-04:00"></time></a></span> <span cl=
ass=3D"post-author">by <a href=3D"https://lovelettertocolumbus.com/author/j=
asonwp/" rel=3D"author">Jason McGathey</a></span> <span class=3D"post-comme=
nts">=E2=80=94 <a href=3D"https://lovelettertocolumbus.com/victorians-midni=
ght-cafe/#respond">Leave a comment</a></span><h1 class=3D"entry-title">Vict=
orian=E2=80=99s Midnight Cafe</h1>		</header><!-- .entry-header -->
				<div class=3D"entry-content">
		<img width=3D"1404" height=3D"1408" src=3D"https://lovelettertocolumbus.c=
om/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/IMG_20250429_0001.jpg" class=3D"attachment- s=
ize- wp-post-image" alt=3D"Songs for Victorian's mix CD 2006" decoding=3D"a=
sync" fetchpriority=3D"high"><meta name=3D"monetization" content=3D"$ilp.up=
hold.com/ziY69pnJyq6X"><p>Victorian=E2=80=99s Midnight Cafe was a former=E2=
=80=A6well, I don=E2=80=99t even know what you=E2=80=99d <em>call </em>it, =
but it sure was something. A cafe, yes, I suppose, and definitely located i=
n Victorian=E2=80=99s Village. And though I was certainly there past midnig=
ht on occasion, those times were rare =E2=80=93 and yet I still might have =
classified it, for a few years there, as the most interesting place to visi=
t in all of Columbus. <em>Cafe </em>at some point morphed into this meaning=
less all-purpose term applied to just about any spot, equally at home on th=
e floor of a dance club as to a quaint diner two seat table that is only op=
en for brunch. And Victorian=E2=80=99s encompassed nearly every plot point =
between these extremes as well as anywhere ever did.</p><p>It wasn=E2=80=99=
t just the mismatched furniture and similarly inclined artwork, the weather=
beaten floors. Or the patrons you could also often apply some of those modi=
fiers to. It was a certain <em>vibe</em> you couldn=E2=80=99t get anywhere =
else =E2=80=93 in large part because even those running this enterprise kep=
t the borders fuzzy, as far as what Victorian=E2=80=99s was even supposed t=
o be. But then again, they weren=E2=80=99t afraid to draw the line at what =
they absolutely were NOT: owner Greg Rowe usually told people who were hopi=
ng to bring CDs in here and have it cranked over the system to politely for=
get it, even when other bars would often play ball with such a concept. Or =
back when, though it=E2=80=99s hard to really fathom this now, you could pr=
etty much smoke cigarettes <em>everywhere </em>(places really only started =
going smoke free en masse somewhere in the mid aughts, a concept that proba=
bly seems as alien to youngsters now as this mysterious =E2=80=9Ccompact di=
sc=E2=80=9D music playing medium I just mentioned), Victorian=E2=80=99s was=
 a notable outlier in that it was always forbidden here. They do have at le=
ast one pool table here, covering yet another base in that regard. </p><p> =
I once brought my brother in for breakfast, and he is still known to gush a=
bout it, specifically the corned beef hash, twenty years later. Connie Harr=
is and Za Hansen are among the cooks who pass through here, during its spir=
ited run under Rowe, and the signature morning offering might actually be a=
 heaping casserole named Mr. Gut Wrencher: eggs, gravy, home fries, cheese,=
 three kinds of meat in one large dish. =E2=80=9CThat scared the hell out o=
f me the first time I read the ingredients,=E2=80=9D Hansen admits, in a Ma=
y 2008 <em>Dispatch </em>piece, =E2=80=9Cfirst I thought, <em>why?, </em>an=
d then I wondered, <em>do we even have a plate big enough for this thing?</=
em>=E2=80=9C</p><p>Well before that, in fact before I=E2=80=99d ever set fo=
ot inside the place, a coworker once secured some of us a slot to play at t=
heir open stage jam night, though I chickened out and failed to show =E2=80=
=93 though assuredly no great loss for anyone involved, whether performer o=
r attendee, I still sometimes regret not following through. Because of cour=
se they had live music here, too. This place was a local institution for su=
ch, with for example the various members of Cowboy Hillbilly Hippy Folk mee=
ting one another here, after which Victorian=E2=80=99s was only the most na=
tural choice for their CD release party. The Moops played their first show =
here in 2001. Of course, unlike many =E2=80=9Copen stage=E2=80=9D jam night=
s I=E2=80=99ve attended over the years, the Victorian=E2=80=99s take on thi=
s meant that during the Thursday night edition, poetry readings were totall=
y okay, too, if that=E2=80=99s how one chose to fill his/her slot =E2=80=93=
 Wednesays are reserved for acoustic music alone.</p><p>So once again total=
ly fitting the Midnight Cafe aesthetic. But yeah, I would say music mostly =
prevailed anyway, on balance. When I introduced Damon to Victorian=E2=80=99=
s, to catch some other random band on an equally random night, he was insta=
ntly a fan and remarked that a place like this could only exist in Columbus=
. As those in charge of the operation are quite aware, considering the top =
of their website home page describes this cafe, in a dictionary style defin=
ition entry, as =E2=80=9C<em>an eclectic home for people wanted or unwanted=
. Loyal patrons refer to her as the =E2=80=9Chub of weirdness=E2=80=9D wher=
e all walks of life come and go. A refreshing gateway from reality, a place=
 to find a warm smile and friendship.=E2=80=9D </em>Yep, that pretty much s=
ums it up. </p><p>Incidentally, their website offers yet another punctuatio=
n plot twist that I didn=E2=80=99t expect. Working on this Love Letter To C=
olumbus project has, however improbably and unwittingly, often thrust me in=
to the role of an apostrophe detective (there=E2=80=99s two words you never=
 thought you=E2=80=99d see together). And so I am presented with another ca=
se here. In every single article I referenced online (47 of them) and in my=
 own writings, thoughts, whatever, the name is never spelled as anything bu=
t Victorian=E2=80=99s Midnight Cafe. I never even entertained a notion that=
 it could be anything else. However, much like other defunct operations suc=
h as <a href=3D"https://lovelettertocolumbus.com/brewery-district/#Brewmast=
ersGate">Brewmasters Gate</a> and <a href=3D"https://lovelettertocolumbus.c=
om/brewery-district/#TommyKeegans">Tommy Keegans</a>, the conflicting truth=
 is hiding in plain sight =E2=80=93 either that, or we have to assume that =
<em>we </em>know what the founders of these operations truly intended, and =
they just weren=E2=80=99t polished up on their grammar. Because according t=
o the logo at the top of the VMC website, which runs unchanged for years, i=
t=E2=80=99s actually spelled with an apostrophe after the S: Victorians=E2=
=80=99 Midnight Cafe. Although in this instance these waters are certainly =
further muddied when you consider the abbreviation, the logo inside the log=
o, which calls this place Vic=E2=80=99s. And <em>then </em>the =E2=80=9Cdic=
tionary definition=E2=80=9D beside it as spells this as Victorian=E2=80=99s=
. These three variations are, what, an inch or even less apart. So I=E2=80=
=99m really not sure what to think. But crafting a logo you would think has=
 to take more time than typing words on a web page =E2=80=93 even back in 2=
004 =E2=80=93 so it would seem more thought had to have gone into that as w=
ell, and the logo therefore carries more weight.</p><figure class=3D"wp-blo=
ck-image size-large"><img data-recalc-dims=3D"1" decoding=3D"async" width=
=3D"980" height=3D"483" src=3D"https://i0.wp.com/lovelettertocolumbus.com/w=
p-content/uploads/2025/05/Victorians-home-page-Jan-2006-watermarked.jpg?res=
ize=3D980%2C483&amp;ssl=3D1" alt=3D"" class=3D"wp-image-15089"></figure><p>=
I guess maybe in the name of keeping a clear conscience, I should refuse to=
 take on this truly baffling case. </p><h3 class=3D"wp-block-heading"><stro=
ng>II.</strong></h3><p>Sometimes Vic=E2=80=99s was even open on Thanksgivin=
g, serving a customarily funky meal that had nothing to do with your tradit=
ional Turkey Day offerings =E2=80=93 and sounding no less inviting because =
of it. Circa 2006 meanwhile, on most totally normal nights of the week, the=
re was this cute redheaded waitress, her belly swollen and many months alon=
g with child, working here, that us guys all agreed was =E2=80=9Cthe hottes=
t pregnant chick ever.=E2=80=9D And the reason I=E2=80=99m coming here so o=
ften then stems from my greatest stretch of involvement with Victorian=E2=
=80=99s, strollling through these extremely funky doors roughly once per we=
ek, as a central figure in this writer=E2=80=99s club we=E2=80=99d started.=
</p><p>Nathan McKnight (a pen name, BTW), his friend Shannon, our mutual pa=
l Dan Bandman, and I are the four who materialize here for its first ever m=
eeting, in January 2006. Bandman is the one who told me about it, and as I=
=E2=80=99d been trying in vain the entire time I lived in Columbus =E2=80=
=93 nearly a decade at this point =E2=80=93 to catch on with a decent write=
r=E2=80=99s club, I=E2=80=99m instantly all about it. I guess it somehow ne=
ver occurred to me to just start one myself. In a hilarious stroke of just =
about the most predictable cliche ever, three of us bring our copy of <em>T=
he Elements Of Style </em>to this first meeting =E2=80=93 and the fourth pe=
rson almost did, but decided to leave it at home. </p><p>Nathan was here ev=
ery single week, though, and deserves credit for organizing the thing, keep=
ing it together for a solid year (possibly more, as I moved away at end of =
2006, and have no idea what happened beyond that point). I made it a good 9=
0% of the time, I would estimate, easily the second most involved. Nathan=
=E2=80=99s dad, Joe, would eventually become a predictable attendee, and wh=
ile both Dan and Shannon were only intermittently engaged, moving forward, =
other highly random figures like Rob, Alison, and Brad would pop in on occa=
sion, in descending order of frequency, culled from whatever rock we could =
find them under. One or two of them might not even have really been writers=
, or at least weren=E2=80=99t writing much, but liked to soak up the atmosp=
here and debate things anyway, possibly take a stab at editing a copy of wh=
atever you brought.</p><p>Some of these conversations stick with me to this=
 day. Like a passionate extended group argument one night, in that window s=
eating area section, concerning the use of the word <em>habit, </em>which s=
omeone was claiming didn=E2=80=99t fit in such and such scenario. We had ju=
st about settled the debate, agreeing that it was basically applicable in s=
ituations where a person couldn=E2=80=99t stop doing something often. Until=
 some guy piped up and wondered, =E2=80=9Cyeah, but would you say robbing b=
anks is a <em>habit?</em>=E2=80=9D Which set the argument ablaze all over a=
gain. Another time, I brought a then short story where the main character k=
illed himself at the very end. A plot twist which Shannon was quite vocal a=
bout not liking.</p><p>=E2=80=9CI just don=E2=80=99t remember ever reading =
a story where the main character killed himself at the end, though,=E2=80=
=9D I pointed out. </p><p>=E2=80=9CThere=E2=80=99s a reason you=E2=80=99ve =
never read a story like that =E2=80=93 it pisses people off!=E2=80=9D</p><p=
>Well, I ended up using this scene anyway, eventually, in one of my novels.=
 So who knows. These philosophical dustups were always highly entertaining,=
 at least, even if you didn=E2=80=99t take the advice. And some of this stu=
ff was demonstrably helpful. Another occasion, Dan brought a ton of song ly=
rics to the table, and was lamenting that he kept trying to squeeze in more=
 adjectives, but they never seemed to rhythmically fit into the songs. I su=
ggested in response that instead of adjective cramming, which a lot of peop=
le try to do in whatever they=E2=80=99re writing, it=E2=80=99s usually bett=
er to come up with <em>stronger verbs </em>instead, like replacing the word=
s <em>go </em>and <em>went </em>et cetera whenever you see them. Nathan=E2=
=80=99s mouth was open, because he was just about to say the exact same thi=
ng, but I beat him to the punch. So he agreed with me, as we elaborated on =
this point. Then the next week, Dan proudly brought his revised songs to th=
e meeting, and was effusive in praising us, because he felt like that one t=
ip had made a huge improvement on his lyric writing.</p><p>I would eventual=
ly conclude that although these meetings were a lot of fun, and gave me som=
ething to look forward to every week, they were ultimately not that product=
ive for me. And the reason for this was that I felt I=E2=80=99d advanced be=
yond everyone else on the seriousness front. It might sound a bit pompous t=
o declare, but I wasn=E2=80=99t thinking this from a quality or talent stan=
dpoint, because most of them were great writers. They just weren=E2=80=99t =
doing much, which was the whole issue. Whereas I couldn=E2=80=99t seem to s=
top, even back then, and was cranking out reams of material, writing <em>so=
mething </em>just about every day. I had an endless stockpile of material I=
 could and sometimes did bring for them to dissect, passing copies out to e=
veryone who attended. But then would feel like I was hogging the spotlight,=
 so might skip a week, except then there would be times where nobody brough=
t <em>anything </em>as a result. </p><p>Plus, as previously alluded to, wou=
ld typically not apply any of their notes anyway. I could get into debating=
 philosophies and word usage and so on until the end of time, though in gen=
eral believed that as a rule you couldn=E2=80=99t really carpet bomb any of=
 these strategies onto every piece of writing, or anything near it, because=
 every piece was different and we all had such diverse styles on top of it.=
 Like I recall that after some of us attended this <a href=3D"https://lovel=
ettertocolumbus.com/2006-personal-journal/#March01">Kurt Vonnegut speaking =
appearance</a>, where he was ranting and raving about semi-colons, Nathan s=
howed up at the next meeting and proudly announced that he=E2=80=99d gotten=
 rid of 63 semi-colons in something he was writing. And I was thinking, wel=
l, that=E2=80=99s cool, but that=E2=80=99s just never going to be me. Vonne=
gut might have felt they should be eradicated from the face of the planet, =
and Nathan might have agreed, but I thought and continued to feel that they=
 are occasionally quite useful.</p><p>My fondest memory probably concerns a=
 session where I brought this thinly-veiled =E2=80=9Cfictional=E2=80=9D pie=
ce about the Mansfield area music scene, which had Bandman howling with lau=
ghter at various points. He loved it so much he was praising it later to pe=
ople who didn=E2=80=99t even come to these things, like for instance Travis=
 Tyo=E2=80=99s girlfriend Martha. She came up to me somewhere, weeks later =
I believe it was, and told me that whatever I had written, Bandman thought =
it was hysterical.</p><p>The picture up top, meanwhile, stems from a mix CD=
 Nathan once brought to everyone in attendance. He did this at least twice,=
 because I have another one titled <em>Jug O=E2=80=99 Tunes </em>that I lik=
ed so much I made copies of it myself to pass around. <em>Songs For Victior=
ians </em>as you can see is pretty solid, too, and a number of those tracks=
 have entered my permanent playlist as a result. And on exactly one instanc=
e, I cranked out a mix of my own, which I titled <em>J-Mac=E2=80=99s Spring=
 Mix 2000 and 6. </em>Those discs I foisted on this club to start with, tho=
ugh eventually expanding outward and handing them off to the likes of Kevin=
 Spain or my brother, people who had never come to any of these meetings. <=
/p><p>Nathan had some experience organizing these things, and in fact a pre=
vious club was so organized and serious that they were printing impressivel=
y professional looking zines for a while. He brought me a couple-few issues=
 at some point, though I only seem to have one in my possession now. He=E2=
=80=99s also one of these guys who seems to know everybody in town, to the =
extent I wasn=E2=80=99t exactly surprised to eventually discover he was <em=
>working </em>with Damon=E2=80=99s sister, Melissa, at one of her jobs, a s=
hort while after I left town and this writing club had ended. When I asked =
her if she knew Nathan McKnight, she chuckled and said, =E2=80=9Cwell, he m=
ight <em>wish </em>his name was Nathan McKnight=E2=80=A6but yeah, I know hi=
m.=E2=80=9D </p><p>It was only then that I even learned this was a pen name=
! You might say I=E2=80=99m bad at asking people questions about themselves=
. Well, actually, I feel like I=E2=80=99m good at observing some stuff, not=
ing various details about people, and learning a bit of their history =E2=
=80=93 it=E2=80=99s just the material I get down isn=E2=80=99t necessarily =
important. A kink which this Victorian=E2=80=99s writing club never did str=
aighten out.</p><figure class=3D"wp-block-image size-full"><img data-recalc=
-dims=3D"1" decoding=3D"async" width=3D"965" height=3D"931" src=3D"https://=
i0.wp.com/lovelettertocolumbus.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Victorians-pi=
ece-5-3-06.jpg?resize=3D965%2C931&amp;ssl=3D1" alt=3D"Smuggler's Cove early=
 draft with suggested edits" class=3D"wp-image-15062"><figcaption class=3D"=
wp-element-caption">A sample of Nathan=E2=80=99s edits (in green) of a shor=
t story I brought to the group. I did use some of his suggestions on this o=
ne.</figcaption></figure><h3 class=3D"wp-block-heading"><strong>III.</stron=
g></h3><p>I still possess some of the pieces that others brought to this gr=
oup, but haven=E2=80=99t had much luck getting their blessing to post them =
here. So the above snippet from one of my short stories will have to suffic=
e, to give you an idea of the work we did here. </p><p>The final occasions =
I came to Victorian=E2=80=99s all occurred in 2008, the absolute last of th=
ese a bar-hopping odyssey marking my return to Columbus, during which we wo=
und up here for a spell. That night was also, to date, sadly the last time =
too that I=E2=80=99ve hung out with such disparate characters as Alan Kline=
, Ancie and Dan Schmidt, Kevin Spain and others, all of which were among th=
is Victorian=E2=80=99s entourage that night. Though it seems most surreal o=
f all to recall this was the site of my first conversation in 19 years with=
 on old friend who=E2=80=99d moved away, Byron McClurg, because he had call=
ed someone, and a few of us were passing around the phone on the back patio=
 here.</p><p>From here the picture becomes a little murkier. In March =E2=
=80=9909 it=E2=80=99s announced that local musician Andreas Kleinert has bo=
ught the place, along with his wife, Kristy Venrick, and that they are rena=
ming it Vic=E2=80=99s Cafe. It is closed a short spell for remodeling, alth=
ough they maintain many of the same employees, even some menu standouts lik=
e weinerschnitzel or the Behemoth Burger. A continued or perhaps slightly e=
levated devotion to live music, six nights a week, including open stage jam=
s on three of those. Yet they are also switching gears, somewhat, like with=
 a curious focus on a lengthy pina colada list (or is this not playing righ=
t into the site=E2=80=99s scattershot, eclectic vibe?) including one that=
=E2=80=99s served in a coconut shell.</p><p>And yet by July, it would appea=
r they=E2=80=99ve reverted back to the former name, Victorian=E2=80=99s Mid=
night Cafe, though closing right at midnight on every night not named Frida=
y or Saturday. Even so the last event listing I can find occurs in March 20=
10, a fundraiser in support of and featuring local musician Billy Zenn. Sho=
rtly thereafter, those owners sold it to the next, and whoever bought this =
now not only changed the name but the entire aesthetic as well. One night i=
n 2011, Kyle, Erin, and I drifted through the new establishment, which was =
like this voodoo rockabilly place called The Shrunken Head. And while cool =
enough for that sort of thing, it was also just not the same, and none of u=
s ever came back. Nowadays this spot, at 251 W. 5th Avenue, is known as the=
 Vic Village Tavern. This one=E2=80=99s rocking some old school vibe, and I=
=E2=80=99m sure it has its adherents, but it also looks even more normal an=
d therefore farther removed still from what once made this spot on the map =
so special.</p><p>I said their website was hilariously generic, even by the=
 standards of that time, and this is true. A plain white background, no pho=
tos whatsoever, text even more basic than my somewhat vanilla choices here =
in the year 2025. If visiting that page, you would have <em>no idea </em>wh=
at a wacky establishment you were in store for, should you follow up with a=
 physical visit. However one cool feature they did have, which I haven=E2=
=80=99t quite seen replicated anywhere else, is that they also made a runni=
ng list of every musician they could think of who graced their stage. So he=
re=E2=80=99s the roll call up through 2006:</p><p><br>Amy Steinberg<br>Andy=
